title: Fuse the lists without tuning a dozen knobs
brief: Two ranked lists disagree. One speaks BM25 and one speaks cosine, and their scores sit on different scales. How do you merge them, and when is the zero-tuning default the wrong choice?

blocks.text: Why ranks travel better than scores

blocks.md:
BM25 `@search.score` has no upper limit. Cosine similarity in Azure AI Search runs from 0.333 to 1.00. The semantic ranker reports `@search.rerankerScore` from 0 to 4 after fusion, separately from both [[r1]]. Adding raw numbers across those scales lets whichever list has bigger numbers win.

**Reciprocal rank fusion** sidesteps the problem by using only the rank each list gives a document. Azure AI Search applies it whenever two or more queries run in parallel: a text query plus one vector query is 2 executions, one vector query on two vector fields makes 3, and two vector queries over five vector fields make 11 [[r1]]. Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher fixed `k = 60` in a pilot on TREC data and reported that the exact choice was not critical [[r9]].

blocks.title: Reciprocal rank fusion with optional weights
blocks.expr: RRF(d) = sum over lists i of  w_i / (k + rank_i(d))

vars.v: position of document d in list i, starting at 1 (a missing document adds 0)
a constant, 60 in the original paper. It is not the neighbour count `k` of a vector query
per-list weight, default 1.0. In Azure it is `vectorQueries[].weight`

blocks.example: At `k = 60`, rank 1 contributes 1/61 = 0.0164 and rank 50 contributes 1/110 = 0.0091. Two lists can give at most 2/61 = **0.0328**, which is why fused scores look tiny. Only their order matters.

items.label: RRF constant k
items.note: Cormack 2009 pilot and the Elasticsearch rank_constant default. Azure says a small value such as 60, and the exact value it uses is not stated.

items.label: Default hybrid result count
items.note: Top 50 of the fused set when you do not page.

items.label: Default vector query weight
items.note: The Azure example uses 0.5 and 2.0 to bias one query.

blocks.intro: Load the three presets (exact identifier, conceptual paraphrase, mixed query), then run the guided experiments under What to notice. On the mixed query, document D10 is first in the vector list only: watch where it lands at k = 1, 60 and 200.

blocks.title: Fusion functions
blocks.intro: Pick the function by what you can measure, not by what is fashionable.

options.name: Reciprocal rank fusion
options.summary: Sum of weight / (k + rank) over lists.
cons: Throws away score gaps: a runaway first hit and a near tie look alike
Bruch et al. found it sensitive to its parameters
options.bestWhen: You have no labels yet, the lists use different scales, or you fuse several vector queries.
options.avoidWhen: Score gaps carry signal and you have labelled queries to tune against.

options.name: Convex combination of normalised scores
options.summary: Normalise each list's scores, then take a weighted sum with weights adding to 1.
pros: Beat RRF in and out of domain in Bruch et al.
Needed only a small labelled set
cons: Normalisation choice matters, and one outlier score can squash a list
Needs scores you can trust, so a labelled check is mandatory
options.bestWhen: You have a few hundred labelled queries and stable scores.
options.avoidWhen: Scores are not exposed by the engine or you cannot label anything.

options.name: Fuse, then rerank
options.summary: Use any cheap fusion for recall, then let a reranker decide the final order.
pros: Reranker reads full text, so fusion quality matters less
Fits the funnel of the next level
cons: Adds a model hop and cost
Only as good as the candidate set
options.bestWhen: Latency allows one more stage and precision at the top matters.
options.avoidWhen: The budget is a single fast query.

items.symptom: Fused results look like the vector list only.
items.cause: Raw scores were summed or min-max normalised, and one BM25 outlier squashed the keyword list toward 0.
items.fix: Fuse by rank, or normalise with a method that resists outliers. Replay a query with a runaway score as a regression test.

items.symptom: A document first in one list sits below documents found by both.
items.cause: With k = 60 agreement outweighs a single top rank. That is the design, not a bug.
items.fix: If top-rank trust is wrong for your data, lower k or raise that list's weight, and measure the change.

items.symptom: Raising `k` in a hybrid request does not change how ranks are weighted in fusion.
items.cause: The vector query `k` is the neighbour count, not the RRF constant, which has no documented request parameter.
items.fix: Tune the per-query `weight` and `maxTextRecallSize` instead, and name the two k values separately in reviews.

items.symptom: Recall drops after adding a weak third list.
items.cause: Each extra list adds noise and its own top-rank points at equal weight.
items.fix: Weight it below the others, or remove it. Slice recall by query class before and after.

blocks.title: Azure details that trip people up
blocks.md: Weights are GA. `maxTextRecallSize` is a **preview** parameter (2026-08-01-preview, checked 2026-10-13). The vector `threshold` parameter is preview too and drops weak matches before fusion even if fewer than `k` remain [[r35]]. Elasticsearch exposes the constant as `rank_constant` with a default of 60 and a `rank_window_size` that defaults to the request size [[r32]]. OpenAI file search takes `embedding_weight` and `text_weight` under `ranking_options.hybrid_search` [[r30]].

quiz.q: With `k = 60` and equal weights, a document is rank 4 in the keyword list and rank 2 in the vector list. What is its RRF score?
quiz.explain: 1/64 = 0.015625 and 1/62 = 0.016129, so the sum is 0.031754, about 0.0318. Ranks start at 1 and the constant is added to the rank, so using rank 3 and 1 as zero-based positions gives a different, wrong number.

quiz.q: Document A is rank 1 in one list only. Document B is rank 10 in both lists. Which setting makes A outscore B?
quiz.explain: At k = 1, A scores 1/2 = 0.5 and B scores 2/11 = 0.18, so A wins. At k = 60, A is 0.0164 and B is 0.0286, and at k = 200 A is 0.0050 and B is 0.0095, so agreement wins. Small k trusts top ranks and large k trusts agreement, so a value of k does exist.

quiz.q: A team reports that their hybrid results are almost identical to BM25 alone. What is wrong with this fusion code?
options: It sums raw scores from different scales, so the larger scale dominates
It should sort ascending, because a lower fused score means a better match
It must divide each total by the number of lists before sorting the documents
It should start from a default of 1 instead of 0 for documents missing from a list
quiz.explain: BM25 scores are unbounded and cosine scores sit between 0.333 and 1.00, so adding them lets BM25 decide. Fix it with rank-based fusion or normalised scores. Sorting ascending would invert relevance, dividing by the list count rescales every document the same, and a default of 1 adds a constant to every missing list entry.

quiz.q: Select every situation in which a tuned convex combination is a better bet than RRF.
options: A small labelled query set is available to tune the weight
There are no labels and no time to create any
Your own evaluation shows RRF results swing when k or the weights change
You will not normalise scores and the engine does not expose them
quiz.explain: Bruch et al. found convex combination beat RRF and needed only a small labelled set, and they found RRF sensitive to its parameters, so evidence of that on your data points the same way. With no labels you cannot tune the weight, and with unexposed or unnormalised scores convex combination cannot run, so RRF is the fallback.

takeaways: RRF fuses ranks, so BM25 and cosine never need to share a scale
Small k trusts top ranks and large k trusts agreement between lists
The RRF constant and the vector query k are different things
Convex combination can win when you have a small labelled set, and RRF is the zero-label default
